options: Marks the end of a statement
Starts a single-line comment that runs to the end of the line
Starts a multi-line block comment
Subtracts two values
questions.explain: Everything after -- on that line is ignored by SQL Server.

questions.q: How do you write a comment that spans multiple lines?
options: Start each line with --
Wrap it in ' and '
Wrap it in /* and */
Multi-line comments aren't supported in T-SQL
questions.explain: /* ... */ block comments can span as many lines as needed, unlike -- which only comments to end of line.

questions.q: What should a good comment explain?
options: A word-for-word restatement of each line of code
Only the author's name and the date
Nothing — comments should be avoided entirely
The WHY behind a non-obvious choice, not just what the code already shows
questions.explain: A comment like '-- Select FirstName' adds nothing the code doesn't already say; explaining the reason behind a query is what actually helps future readers.

questions.q: Which formatting convention does this course use for every script from Chapter 1 forward?
options: Lowercase keywords with no punctuation
UPPERCASE keywords, a semicolon on every statement, and USE/GO at the top
Comments are required on every single line
One giant line per query with no line breaks
questions.explain: Consistent formatting (uppercase keywords, semicolons, an opening USE statement, schema.table naming) keeps every script in this course readable the same way.

questions.q: Why does this course open every script with USE <database>; GO?
options: It's required syntax for every T-SQL statement
It's a comment, not executable code
It improves query performance
So the script's target database is unambiguous, regardless of the toolbar dropdown (Lesson 2)
questions.explain: This directly ties back to Lesson 2 — USE sets database context explicitly in the script itself.
